title: A diagonal cuts a corner and one part is known: what is the other?
description: A diagonal cuts the corner of a rectangle into two angles, and one of them is sixty degrees. The video finds the other angle from the whole corner, checks it with a protractor, and breaks Keeko's doubt that a diagonal cuts the corner in half.
teaching_notes: One idea: the two angles at a corner of a rectangle fill a right angle, so take the known one away from ninety degrees. Watch for the slip of thinking the diagonal cuts the corner in half.

source: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two
video_script.why: A learner uses the fact that a corner of a rectangle is a right angle to find one part when the other part is known, and checks it by measuring.
video_script.substitution: the book's rectangle ABCD with the diagonal AC, one part of the angle at A being sixty degrees
video_script.anchor: the book's rectangle ABCD with the diagonal AC cutting the corner at A into two angles
video_script.wrong_answer: the other angle is also sixty degrees
video_script.wrong_move: thinks a diagonal always cuts the corner in half, so both parts must be alike
video_script.payoff_line: The other angle is thirty degrees.

final_answer.spoken: the other angle is thirty degrees

maths_rules: the corner of a rectangle is 90 degrees
the two angles made by the diagonal add up to 90 degrees
check with a protractor: the other angle reads 30 degrees
60 + 60 = 120 degrees, which is more than a right angle, so the doubt cannot hold

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the other angle is also sixty degrees, because the diagonal cuts the corner in half.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But sixty and sixty make one hundred and twenty degrees, which is more than the corner.
<bookmark mark='keep'/>The diagonal cuts the corner in halves only when the two sides are equal.
